To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the network capacity of a single-class system with linear receivers in a fading channel can be expressed as a function of the users' SIR requirements and received power distribution.
the network capacity of imperfectly power-controlled CDMA systems with MF receivers is a function of the users' SIR requirements and the users' received power distributions.

the network capacity of a single-class CDMA system equipped with linear receivers can be expressed uniquely and compactly in terms of the target SIRs and the received power distributions, and that the network capacity is maximized when the received powers are matched to the users' target SIRs.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the admissibility, network capacities, and power control of imperfect power-controlled CDMS systems.
the admissibility of imperfect power-controlled CDMAS in fading environments.
the admissibility, network capacities, and effective target SIRs and effective bandwidths of imperfect power-controlled CD MA systems in fading channels, with MF and linear receivers.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, in fading environments, imperfect power control is more detrimental to the network capacity of CDMA systems than the fading channel itself.

for the random signature cases, the network capacities are uniquely determined by the users' SIR requirements and received power profiles, and that for the deterministic signature cases, the admissibility is determined by the users’ SIR requirements and effective target SIRs.

for imperfect power-controlled CD MA systems with MF receivers, the network capacity is uniquely determined by the SIR requirements and the received power distributions, and the admissibility is determined by the S IR requirements and the effective target SIR, which is determined by the received power distributions.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the network capacity of an admissible system is the maximum number, over all possible power distributions, of users whose SIR requirements are met with the given power distributions.
the admissibility of a single-class system with linear receivers in a fading environment can be uniquely determined by the effective target SIR of each user and the effective bandwidth of its signal.

, in fading environments, the network capacity of an admissible system is a function of the users' SIR requirements and received power statistics, regardless of the signature sequence structure and the receiver type.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the network capacity is not necessarily a monotonic function of the users' SIR requirements.
the admissibility of an imperfect powercontrolled CDMA system is not only dependent on the received power distributions, but also on the users' QoS requirements.
a CDMA system with imperfect power control is more robust to fading channels than one with perfect power control, and hence, the former is a better choice in a fading channel.
